task.goal: Make a small street-fair quiet zone useful without separating visitors by disability label.
hard_constraints: One tent, two volunteers and paper signs; no extra staff or permanent structure.
Access must be voluntary and available to anyone; no collection of diagnoses.
Compare use, crowd spillover and volunteer effort over two afternoons.
task.expected_result: A dignified quiet-space layout and trial.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the site layout to shelter a quiet pocket
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is reducing exposure to passing crowds through tent placement, orientation and seating. Use the site plan to identify a permitted location away from speakers and queues, while keeping the tent visible from a main route. Face the entrance away from the busiest flow and arrange existing seats toward the quieter outlook, leaving a clear, accessible entrance and turning space. Paper signs at the approach and entrance say: “Quiet rest space — everyone welcome. Come and go freely.” Do not identify users by disability or ask why they enter.

One volunteer welcomes visitors without requiring conversation; the other monitors the approach and redirects fair queues that obstruct access. Both can support visitors when needed. The proposal assumes organizers permit repositioning the tent and that the site offers a meaningfully quieter orientation. A tent provides little sound insulation, so placement may offer only modest relief. Avoid hidden corners, blocked sightlines and locations that make the space hard to find.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both afternoons, alternate comparable observation periods between ordinary perimeter seating and the sheltered orientation, keeping the welcome signs and available seats constant. Reconfigure only when visitors have left voluntarily. Volunteers record anonymous entry totals, occupied-seat snapshots, instances of people or queues obstructing the approach, and minutes spent welcoming, redirecting or rearranging. Offer an optional spoken question: “Was this restful enough?” No personal information is recorded. The mechanism is doubtful if the sheltered arrangement produces no clearer reports of relief while increasing access obstructions or volunteer effort. Record nearby performances and weather changes; this small trial cannot reliably separate their effects.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make quiet a shared activity rather than an identity
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is a clear, universal agreement about behavior inside the tent. A welcoming sign reads: “Quiet break — open to everyone. Please pause conversations and silence phone audio. No need to explain your visit.” Visitors may leave whenever they wish. This defines the space by what people do there, with no disability label or eligibility judgment.

Arrange existing seats with generous passage space and several seating directions so conversation is optional. One volunteer offers a brief welcome when useful; the second monitors the boundary and suggests that conversations continue outside the entrance, away from the access route. Use gentle reminders, never demands that distressed visitors suppress involuntary sounds. The space promises reduced conversation and amplified audio, not complete silence.

This requires visitors to understand and mostly follow the signs, and volunteers to feel comfortable making respectful reminders. It will have limited value if nearby music dominates the sound or if reminders themselves become intrusive. Use the existing tent, seating and paper signs only.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During each of two afternoons, alternate comparable periods using a general “Rest space — everyone welcome” sign and the explicit quiet agreement, keeping location and seating unchanged. Assume an ordinary clock is available for equal observation periods. Record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, audible conversations or phone audio, conversations displaced into the entrance route, and volunteer minutes and reminder counts. Ask willing departing visitors whether they could rest comfortably, without asking about diagnoses. The agreement is not supported if disruptive sound remains similar, or any improvement comes with frequent correction, reduced use or greater crowd obstruction. Treat differences as provisional because visitors and fair activity will vary between periods.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep a few seats genuinely available through voluntary turnover
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is protecting access to scarce seating by encouraging brief, renewable rests when demand is high. Set up the tent with existing seats and an unobstructed entrance. Signs say: “Rest here — everyone welcome. When others are waiting, please consider sharing a seat after a short break. Stay longer if you need.” Visitors choose whether to enter, leave or continue resting; volunteers do not assess need, enforce time limits or collect diagnoses.

One volunteer welcomes visitors and explains seat availability. The second watches for waiting visitors and crowd spillover. When seats are full, give a general, occasional reminder to the whole tent, without singling anyone out. Offer waiting visitors clear information and invite them to return; do not form a queue across a walkway. Never exceed the tent’s safe capacity.

This approach assumes seats sometimes remain occupied after visitors feel ready to move on and that a courteous prompt can release them. It cannot create capacity when everyone still needs their seat. Its principal risk is making visitors feel hurried, so comfort and freedom to stay are essential checks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both afternoons, alternate comparable periods with a simple open-rest welcome and with the voluntary sharing message. Keep seating, location and quiet expectations constant. Record anonymous entries, occupied-seat snapshots, people who approach but cannot find a seat, waiting groups obstructing circulation, and volunteer minutes spent explaining or prompting. Ask willing departing visitors: “Did you feel free to stay as long as you needed?” Stop prompting if visitors report pressure. The mechanism fails if seat access does not improve, waiting merely shifts outside the tent, or visitors feel hurried. Compare both afternoons and note event changes; increased turnover alone does not establish a better quiet space.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Create quieter intervals by reducing sound at its source
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is temporarily reducing nearby amplified sound so the tent offers actual acoustic relief. A tent provides little sound insulation; cooperation from the nearest sound source could therefore matter more than changes inside it.

Use the site plan to identify the tent location and nearby amplified activities. Before the trial, ask organizers whether existing sound operators can provide agreed lower-volume intervals during both afternoons, without adding staff. This alternative requires a controllable sound source, operator cooperation and permission; if these are unavailable, it is not feasible within the resources.

Keep the tent open throughout, with existing seating, a clear accessible entrance and space beside seats for mobility devices or companions. Paper signs read: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. Come and go freely. No explanation needed.” A second sign lists agreed quieter intervals while explaining that fair sounds remain audible. Visitors can use the space outside those intervals too. Nobody is classified by disability or asked for a diagnosis.

One volunteer supports access and observes use; the other watches the approach and records crowd interference. Existing sound operators make only the agreed adjustments as part of their normal duties. Reduced sound may benefit surrounding visitors as well, but quieter intervals could attract enough demand to overwhelm the tent. Uncontrolled music, generators or traffic may also erase the benefit.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
On each afternoon, compare equal ordinary-volume and agreed lower-volume periods with the same tent layout, signs and seating. Reverse their order on the second afternoon and, where possible, compare periods within the same performance. Record anonymous entry totals, occupied-seat snapshots, blocked-path observations, and volunteer minutes spent assisting or managing spillover. Separately record coordination time. Ask willing departing visitors: “Could you get a restful break?” Record only answer totals.

The mechanism lacks support if lower-volume periods do not improve reported rest, or if crowd spillover and volunteer effort make the benefit impractical. Note performance, weather and attendance differences; two afternoons provide a feasibility check, not reliable causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make the quiet break predictable and self-directed
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is reducing uncertainty and social demands: visitors can understand how to use the tent before entering, without negotiating with a volunteer. This could make a short rest easier for anyone who feels overwhelmed, tired or reluctant to ask for help.

Use paper signs to show a simple seating diagram and explain what happens inside: “Quiet break — everyone welcome. Choose any available place. No check-in or conversation needed. Come and go freely. Fair sounds remain audible.” Mark the entrance and exit on the diagram, using the same opening if necessary. Include “For help, approach either volunteer.” Use large, plain lettering and a few simple symbols.

Arrange existing seats with a clear passage and room for someone using a mobility device to rest beside a companion. Both volunteers remain available near the edge without routinely greeting or questioning entrants; one watches access while the other observes use. They intervene when assistance or safe circulation requires it. No diagnoses or reasons for visiting are requested.

This requires a layout that can be accurately described and signs readable from the approach without blocking it. It assumes uncertainty or expected interaction deters some visitors. Written information will not serve everyone, so quiet verbal help remains available. Predictability cannot overcome dominant fair noise or insufficient seating.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
During each of two afternoons, compare equal periods with a basic “Quiet rest — everyone welcome” sign against periods adding the diagram and explicit self-service information. Reverse the order on afternoon two. Keep seating, quiet expectations and volunteer behavior constant; assume an ordinary clock is available.

Use paper tallies for entries, occupied-seat snapshots, approach obstructions, requests for procedural explanation and volunteer minutes spent assisting or managing spillover. Ask willing departing visitors: “Was it clear how to use this space?” Record answer totals only.

The mechanism is weakened if clarity does not improve or explanation requests remain similar. Reject the arrangement if sign-reading groups obstruct access or volunteer effort rises without a useful improvement in use. Note weather and nearby event changes; two afternoons establish feasibility, not a reliable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Make the quiet space discoverable before visitors need it
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is reducing failed discovery: a well-placed tent cannot help visitors who do not know it exists or cannot find it when tired. Use the site plan to select two nearby decision points where paper arrows can direct people without sending them through queues. Signs read: “Quiet rest tent — everyone welcome,” with an arrow and a recognizable destination description. The entrance repeats the same wording. Do not use disability symbols as eligibility markers.

Place the tent away from major sound sources, arrange existing seats with a clear entrance and turning space, and display a request for low conversation and no phone audio. Entry is voluntary, requires no explanation, and has no registration. One volunteer tends the tent; the other checks the signed approach and handles obstructions. Neither recruits passersby or creates a waiting line.

This requires permission to post paper signs at useful points and a route that is accessible and reasonably direct. Signs must not obstruct circulation. The approach may increase demand beyond the tent’s capacity; the volunteers should explain when seats are full without assessing anyone’s need. Existing occupants remain free to stay. Unlike the prior placement route, this changes whether visitors reach the space, rather than how sheltered they are once inside.
EXPAND.experiment: The tent volunteer owns a two-afternoon trial. On each afternoon, compare equal periods with entrance signage alone against periods with the additional directional signs; reverse the order on afternoon two. Keep placement, seating and quiet expectations fixed. Record anonymous entries, occupied-seat snapshots, approaches when seating is full, walkway obstructions and volunteer minutes spent directing or resolving crowding. At departure, optionally ask whether finding the tent was easy and whether the break helped. Stop the added signage if it repeatedly draws a crowd that the two volunteers cannot clear while maintaining access. More entries alone are insufficient: reject the addition if useful rests do not increase or gains depend on substantially greater effort or spillover. Differences in performances, weather and attendance limit interpretation.

EXPAND.title: Show seating availability before people reach the entrance
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is making a changing resource visible so visitors can choose whether to approach, reducing unsuccessful trips and clustering at the doorway. Place a reversible paper sign at the nearest clear approach: “Seats available” or “All seats occupied — welcome to check again; please keep this route clear.” Explain that availability can change. The sign concerns seating only; it must not imply that standing space is safe or that entry requires permission.

Use the site plan to choose a sign position visible from the tent without blocking a route. Set up existing seating with accessible circulation and retain usable space for visitors who bring their own mobility seating. A separate entrance sign says: “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. No explanation needed.” Ask visitors to keep conversation and phone audio low, while accepting involuntary sounds.

One volunteer welcomes people when needed. The other observes available seating, turns the sign and prevents an entrance queue. Visitors remain free to approach, enter within safe capacity, leave or return. No seats are reserved and no occupants are asked to move on.

This requires a small enough layout for the volunteer to keep the sign reasonably current. Its limits are stale information and visitors interpreting ‘occupied’ as exclusion. Unlike the prior turnover route, it changes information available before arrival rather than asking seated visitors to release capacity.
EXPAND.experiment: The sign volunteer owns matched observation periods across both afternoons, alternating a static welcome sign with the availability sign and reversing the order on day two. Keep the tent layout and quiet agreement constant. Record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, unsuccessful seating approaches, doorway or walkway crowding, sign changes and volunteer minutes. Optional departure feedback asks whether visitors could obtain a useful break. Also tally observed departures prompted by the occupied sign; their unmet need remains uncertain. Stop the status sign if it repeatedly stays inaccurate or visitors treat it as a prohibition on entry despite clarification. Prefer the static sign if the indicator reduces approaches but produces no improvement in access or crowding, or consumes too much volunteer attention. Lower use must not automatically be counted as success.

EXPAND.title: Reduce an avoidable noise source at its origin
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is reducing sound reaching the tent by changing an existing source, addressing a consequential limit of tent orientation: fabric provides little sound insulation. Before opening, one volunteer uses the site plan and a brief listening walk to identify whether a nearby controllable source, such as an event speaker, dominates the proposed rest area. Ask its existing authorized operator whether a small volume reduction or change in speaker direction can preserve the event’s function while reducing sound at the tent. Volunteers do not move equipment or touch controls.

Proceed only if an authorized operator is already present and agrees; this adds no staffing requirement. If no suitable source or willing operator exists, this route is unavailable. Keep emergency announcements and required communications fully functional. Do not redirect sound toward another rest area, neighboring homes or an important pedestrian route.

Set up the single tent with existing seats, clear circulation and a universal paper welcome. Access remains voluntary, with no diagnoses or eligibility questions. One volunteer stays at the tent; the second coordinates the agreed adjustment and checks the affected neighboring area, then returns. Restore the previous setting through the operator if the change causes problems.

Unlike the prior placement route, this reduces incoming sound at its origin. It assumes an adjustable source contributes enough noise for a modest change to matter; without instruments, the magnitude remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: The coordinating volunteer owns a bounded trial with the operator’s agreement. During comparable programmed activity on each of two afternoons, compare the original setting and the agreed adjustment, reversing order on the second afternoon. Keep tent placement, seating and signs fixed. Record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, optional reports of whether visitors could rest, crowd spillover, complaints from the affected neighboring area, and volunteer minutes spent coordinating or checking. Restore the original setting immediately if required communications become less clear or the operator identifies an operational problem. End the trial if coordination repeatedly leaves the entrance inadequately supported. Prefer the simple placement approach if useful rest shows no consistent improvement or any benefit shifts noise elsewhere or requires sustained volunteer effort. Changing acts, attendance and weather may prevent a clear conclusion.

EXPAND.title: Verify the quiet pocket before committing the tent
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the source route “Use the site layout to shelter a quiet pocket.” Preserve its main mechanism: reduce exposure to passing crowds through location, entrance orientation and seating. Add an operational decision before opening: one volunteer listens at the proposed seating area and checks the approach while the other checks a second permitted location on the existing site plan. Compare them during actual fair activity, including whether ordinary conversation remains comfortable and queues leave the entrance clear. This is a practical comparison, not a sound measurement.

Choose the quieter accessible option only if its advantage does not require a concealed entrance or obstructed route. Orient existing seats toward the quieter outlook, retain turning space, and post “Quiet rest — everyone welcome. No explanation needed.” Request low conversation and no phone audio without policing involuntary sounds. One volunteer supports visitors; the other watches the approach.

The changed action closes the source’s unverified prerequisite that a proposed location actually provides relief once the fair starts. If performances or queues later overwhelm it, the approach volunteer checks the alternate location. Move only when the tent is voluntarily empty and the two volunteers can safely handle its existing setup; otherwise retain seating and temporarily label it “Rest space,” explaining the noise limitation when asked. Never interrupt someone’s rest to relocate. If neither location is suitable, make no quietness promise.

This uses one tent, two volunteers, existing seats, the site plan and paper signs. It assumes permitted alternative locations exist; tent fabric itself offers little acoustic protection. The listening check and any move add work, so retain the original location if the benefit is unclear.
EXPAND.experiment:
Both volunteers own a two-afternoon comparison. On afternoon one, assess the source’s proposed layout and record its performance during fixed observation periods. On afternoon two, apply the location decision and recovery procedure, keeping seating quantity and welcome wording consistent except when the fallback label is needed. Do not deliberately expose visitors to a location already judged unsuitable.

Record anonymous entries, occupied-seat snapshots, optional departing feedback on whether the break helped, approach obstructions and displaced queues, and volunteer minutes spent checking, welcoming, redirecting or moving. Record nearby performances and weather. Count closures or moves as lost availability, rather than treating lower crowding during closure as success. Stop relocation attempts if they require extra help, disrupt occupants or compromise access; use the rest-space fallback. Prefer the original arrangement if useful rest does not improve enough to justify the added effort or displaced crowding. Differences between afternoons limit causal conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Keep resting seats comfortable as the shade moves
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: reduce direct sun and heat exposure during a rest, which can make an acoustically quieter tent unusable on a sunny afternoon. This route qualifies only if sun exposure or stuffiness is an observed problem; its benefit in cool or overcast conditions is uncertain.

Use the site plan to choose a permitted location away from speakers and queues, then inspect the tent’s actual shade. Arrange existing seats within the shaded area with open circulation, a clear entrance and room for visitors using their own mobility seating. Leave existing ventilation openings unobstructed. Do not add fabric walls or alter structural fittings. Paper signs say “Quiet shaded rest — everyone welcome. Come and go freely,” and request low conversation and no phone audio while accepting involuntary sounds. Entry requires no explanation or diagnosis.

One volunteer supports visitors. During ordinary approach checks, the second watches for seats becoming exposed to direct sun. That volunteer offers an occupant the option of moving to an available shaded position, and moves empty seats within the established clear area. Occupants may decline; nobody must move to keep the layout tidy. Stop adding or shifting seats when doing so would narrow access, exceed capacity or create a cluster outside the tent.

The decision boundary is actual usable shade, not a fixed seat count. If the tent remains uncomfortable despite shaded seating and open existing ventilation, stop describing it as a cooling refuge and explain the limitation. Do not imply protection from dangerous heat. Compared with a fixed arrangement, this may sustain comfortable rests but can reduce available seats and increase unsuccessful approaches. It needs only the stated resources and assumes the tent casts useful shade.
EXPAND.experiment:
The approach volunteer leads a two-afternoon trial. During comparable periods on each afternoon, compare a fixed shaded seating arrangement with the procedure for moving empty seats as shade changes; reverse the order on afternoon two. Apply the comfort and access stop rules in every period, including the fixed arrangement.

Record entries, occupied-seat snapshots, seats exposed to direct sun, approaches without a usable seat, entrance or walkway spillover, and volunteer minutes spent checking or moving seats. Ask willing departing visitors whether temperature and shade allowed a useful rest; collect no personal information. Note cloud cover and nearby fair activity on the same paper record.

Stop seat movement immediately if it disrupts resting visitors or reduces accessible circulation. Abandon the procedure if it repeatedly consumes attention needed at the entrance. Retain a fixed layout if comfort shows no clear improvement or gains require excessive seat loss, crowd displacement or volunteer effort. This small trial can assess practicality and reported comfort, not establish heat safety.
